anomaly_def.Name: Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly : Engine-level settings (e.g., buffer-pool size, work-memory, checkpoint and log sizing, parallelism caps) are mis-tuned relative to hardware and workload characteristics.
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly : The database process allocates, grows, and retains memory regions beyond the safe physical or virtual limits of the host, triggering OS-level pressure and cache churn.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly : Physical or logical free space for data, log, temp, or backup areas is exhausted, causing allocation failures and blocking persistence operations.

When these three root causes manifest concurrently, the system can exhibit cascading and hard-to-interpret symptoms:  • Erratic wait-event patterns such as log-write or flush waits even while I/O devices are under-utilised, coupled with memory-pressure stalls and sudden OOM terminations.  • Rapid growth of both memory pools and on-disk segments (data, temp, or log) until space ceilings are hit, leading to client-visible "no space left" or "cannot extend" errors.  • Frequent checkpoints and page-flush storms generated by aggressive configuration knobs that flood both RAM and disk, amplifying storage exhaustion while still leaving hot data evicted from caches.  • Node eviction, failover, or restart loops as the engine alternates between memory over-commit, forced checkpoints, and failed log or temp-file extensions.  • Monitoring tools may show contradictory signals—CPU idle yet high latch contention, disks idle then suddenly saturated, memory free then abruptly paged out—making diagnosis non-trivial.

Causal interaction: Mis-set configuration parameters can over-inflate memory allocations (e.g., oversized buffer pools, per-session work memory, or parallel worker buffers), directly triggering the Memory Allocation Anomaly. Excessive in-memory structures force aggressive checkpointing or spill temporary data, increasing redo and temp-file generation that accelerates Storage Space Capacity exhaustion. Conversely, dwindling disk space limits the engine’s ability to recycle logs or grow temp segments, causing it to retain more data in memory and to extend checkpoints more frequently, which feeds back into memory pressure. The escalating memory pressure prompts the engine to flush dirty pages prematurely, generating additional I/O and consuming remaining space faster. As each layer reacts to the stress induced by the others, the database enters a vicious cycle where mis-configuration drives memory bloat, memory bloat drives disk growth, disk exhaustion induces further mis-behaviour of configuration-dependent subsystems, ultimately degrading both throughput and availability.

entry.official_definition: Specifies how long transmitted data may remain unacknowledged before the TCP connection is forcibly closed.
entry.trigger_condition: TCP data sent by PostgreSQL remains unacknowledged longer than tcp_user_timeout on systems supporting TCP_USER_TIMEOUT.
entry.workload_impact: The TCP connection is forcibly closed.
entry.default_behavior: Default value is 0, selecting the operating system default.
entry.cause_analysis: This timeout is usually triggered when connection establishment, authentication exchange, or session activity does not progress within the allowed time budget.
entry.solution_guidance: Check connection lifecycle, client responsiveness, authentication latency, idle-session handling, and whether connection pools are holding stale sessions.
